passage: Placement cell note, Wasim. Suraj, a final-year student who works part-time as a trainee at a printing firm, came in on Tuesday. He spoke quietly and checked the door twice. He said his manager now expects him on Saturdays and Sundays with no extra pay, warns that "your growth will suffer" if he refuses, and tells him to keep it to himself. Suraj is afraid of losing the reference, yet also feels he owes the firm for taking him on. I did not tell him what to do. We read his offer letter together; it lists weekday hours only. I asked him to keep a dated log of each message and each weekend request, and gave him the campus legal-aid clinic's contact and the counsellor's. I asked him not to resign in anger this week. Follow-up on Friday.

qa.q: Which days does the manager now expect Suraj to work with no extra pay?
qa.a: The manager expects Suraj on Saturdays and Sundays with no extra pay.

qa.q: What is Suraj feeling about the firm, and how does the note show it?
qa.a: Suraj is scared and torn: he is afraid of losing the reference yet feels he owes the firm, and he spoke quietly and checked the door twice.

qa.q: What steps did Wasim suggest, and why avoid resigning in anger?
qa.a: Wasim suggested a dated log, reading the offer letter, and contacting the legal-aid clinic and the counsellor; resigning in anger could cost the reference and leave Suraj with no plan.

qa.q: How does Wasim's approach differ from the manager's?
qa.a: Wasim did not tell Suraj what to do and offered records and support, while the manager uses pressure and asks for silence.

grounding: A boss demands unpaid weekends and secrecy with a threat about growth; Suraj is helped to keep records, check the offer letter and seek support before resigning.

passage: The phone buzzed on the accounts-office desk and Mridul's stomach dropped before he read a word. The message from Sir said: "Send the ledger. Now." Same tone as always, and no threat in it. At the next desk, Sumit saw the colour leave his face. "Again?" Sumit asked quietly. "It's my body," Mridul said. "It jumps at every ping." He sent the file, then opened his notebook and drew two columns: things that had really happened (two shouted meetings, one late call) and things his mind said might happen (being sacked tomorrow). The second column was longer. Under it he wrote the start of a safety net: three months of rent set aside, and two contacts at other firms. Sumit slid over a name of an accountant worth calling.

qa.q: What did the message from Sir say?
qa.a: It said, "Send the ledger. Now."

qa.q: What does Mridul's stomach dropping before he read a word suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mridul dreads the boss's messages, and his body reacts before his mind does, which he treats as information.

qa.q: What did Mridul do with his notebook, and how does it help?
qa.a: He listed what had really happened and what his mind said might happen, which helps him separate real risk from imagined risk.

qa.q: How might Sumit see Mridul's reaction?
qa.a: Sumit noticed the colour leave Mridul's face and asked quietly, so Sumit seems concerned and supportive, and offered a name worth calling.

grounding: Mridul dreads his boss's messages, reads the body reaction as information, separates real from imagined risk and starts a safety net.

passage: Maria was still rinsing the tea cups at nine at night when Mr. Rastogi's voice carried down the office, calling her drawings "a child's scribbles" in front of the interns. "Sorry, sir," she said, as usual. At home, her flatmate Simran asked why she kept apologising. "He got me in," Maria said. "Nobody else would have looked at my college. I owe him." "You do owe him thanks," said Simran. "Does that include being shouted at?" Maria stirred her dal and said nothing. She slept badly. Next morning she wrote two lines in her notebook: Thankful that he opened the door. Not okay with "scribbles". She wasn't sure yet what to do with the second line, but she left it on the page.

qa.q: What did Mr. Rastogi call Maria's drawings?
qa.a: He called them "a child's scribbles".

qa.q: Why does Maria keep excusing how Mr. Rastogi treats her?
qa.a: He got her in and she feels she owes him, so thankfulness and hurt are mixed together.

qa.q: How could Maria honour her thanks without accepting the treatment?
qa.a: She can thank him for opening the door and still calmly refuse to be shouted at, for example by asking for feedback in private.

qa.q: How does Simran see Maria's sense of owing?
qa.a: Simran agrees Maria owes thanks but questions whether that includes being shouted at.

grounding: Maria excuses her boss because he helped her get in; she starts to separate thanks for the past from acceptance of the present treatment.

passage:
Monday, 11 p.m. Ishita typed until her fingers shook: a furious email to every colleague on the staff list about the boss who had screamed at her over a typo in front of a client. Her cursor hovered over Send. Her brother Pranav, on the sofa behind her, said, "Write all of it. Just don't press that yet." She saved it as a draft.

Wednesday. She read the draft again. Half of it was true and clear. The other half was just heat, and one line made her wince.

The next Monday. Ishita opened a new email addressed only to HR. Five plain lines, three dates, two exact quotes and one request for a meeting. She pressed Send and felt her shoulders drop. Pranav held out a cup of tea.

qa.q: How many dates were in the email to HR?
qa.a: The email had three dates.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling on Wednesday when she read the draft again?
qa.a: Her feelings were mixed: she saw that half was true and clear, but the other half was just heat and one line made her wince, so the anger had cooled.

qa.q: What did Ishita do differently in the final email?
qa.a: She wrote to HR only, in five plain lines with dates and quotes and a request for a meeting, which keeps the complaint clear and protects her reference.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Ishita's anger that Monday night?
qa.a: Pranav treats the anger as valid when he says to write all of it, but asks her not to press Send yet, perhaps seeing the risk to her.

grounding: Ishita wants to email the whole company in fury, writes and holds it, cools down, then sends one calm documented complaint to HR.

passage: I'm Ayesha, at the next desk in the design team. For weeks Kavitha had looked worn out. Then on Thursday at the tea point I saw her and Rohit talking in low voices. Rohit was showing her notes on his phone; then she showed him hers. I caught "dates", "same words" and "same here", and by the end her shoulders had come down and she laughed once. When I asked later, Kavitha only said, "Facts, not gossip." She told Rohit not to do anything on her account, and he agreed they would only go to HR if both wanted to. I can't say exactly what she feels, and I don't know the whole story, but she looks lighter than she has in a month.

qa.q: Where did Ayesha see Kavitha and Rohit talking?
qa.a: Ayesha saw them at the tea point on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have felt as she compared notes with Rohit?
qa.a: She may have felt relief that it was not just her, since her shoulders came down and she laughed once, though Ayesha admits she cannot say exactly.

qa.q: How can two colleagues support each other in a situation like this?
qa.a: They can share facts and dates rather than gossip, and support each other without pulling anyone into a risky move, as Kavitha and Rohit agreed.

qa.q: How might Rohit have felt while sharing notes?
qa.a: Rohit may also have felt relief at finding he was not alone, since Ayesha heard "same here" and Rohit agreed to go to HR only if both wanted to.

grounding: A coworker admits facing the same treatment and Kavitha and Rohit quietly compare facts, feeling relief without a risky move.

passage: I'm Chinmay. Looking back, the strangest part was the whiplash. In the morning my boss would call my work "the best in the team", and by evening he would say, "Nobody else would hire you, you know that?" I went home dizzy, unable to tell if I was good or hopeless. I stopped seeing friends because he said outside people would distract me. My old college friend Eshaan kept calling anyway. One night Eshaan said, "Send your CV to two places. If he's right, you lose nothing." I did, mostly to prove Eshaan wrong. Both wrote back with interviews. I remember sitting on the bus holding that email and seeing that the praise and the threats were pulling me the same way. I haven't left yet, but I'm no longer only listening to him.

qa.q: What did the boss say about Chinmay's chances of another job?
qa.a: He said nobody else would hire Chinmay.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay feel dizzy by the end of the day?
qa.a: The praise in the morning and the threats by evening left Chinmay unable to tell if the work was good or hopeless.

qa.q: How did Eshaan's suggestion help Chinmay test the boss's claim?
qa.a: Applying to two places tested the claim, and both wrote back with interviews, so the claim was not proven true.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have seen Chinmay's situation from outside?
qa.a: Eshaan kept calling and said Chinmay would lose nothing by applying, which suggests Eshaan saw the claim as untested and worried about Chinmay pulling away from friends.

grounding: A boss alternates praise and threats and says nobody else would hire Chinmay; Chinmay tests the claim by applying elsewhere with an outside friend's help.

passage:
Divyansh texts his friend Mohit during a lunch break.

Divyansh: He made me redo the whole sheet at 9pm again. Called me useless in front of the client.
Mohit: bro just quit
Divyansh: Can't. Papa's medicines and my sister's fees run on my salary. It's not weakness, it's just the maths right now.
Mohit: True. Sorry. So what do you do?
Divyansh: Stay, but not swallow it whole. I keep a note on my phone with dates. I eat lunch away from my desk and switch off at eight even if he pings. Two applications every Sunday.
Mohit: That's an actual plan.
Divyansh: I keep hearing "everyone gets shouted at, it's normal". It's not normal, Mohit. It's just where I am for now.
Mohit: Agreed. This Sunday I'll help with your CV.

qa.q: How many applications does Divyansh send every Sunday?
qa.a: Divyansh sends two applications every Sunday.

qa.q: How does Divyansh feel about staying in the job?
qa.a: Divyansh feels stuck but clear-eyed: quitting is not possible because Papa's medicines and the sister's fees run on the salary, and Divyansh refuses to think of the shouting as normal.

qa.q: How is Divyansh protecting his dignity and health while staying?
qa.a: He keeps dated notes, eats lunch away from his desk, switches off at eight and sends two applications every Sunday, so he is planning a way out.

qa.q: How does Mohit's view change during the chat?
qa.a: Mohit first says to just quit, then accepts the money constraint, calls it an actual plan and offers to help with the CV. 🤍

grounding: Divyansh needs the salary for his family and swallows the abuse, staying while planning a way out and refusing to call it normal.

passage: I'm Rukmini, a designer at the agency. Kamal joined in June as an "intern". He works nine to eight, handles client files on his own, and gets no stipend. When he asked what he would learn, he was told "we'll see about a job later". Last Friday I saw him at the pantry with a small notebook, muttering. He had written two questions for the manager: what stipend, and what learning goals. The manager said, "We'll see." Kamal nodded, smiled tightly and wrote a date at the end of the month in his notebook. I can't tell if he is afraid, angry or just resolved. On Monday I saw him updating his CV in the lunch break, with the agency line still on it.

qa.q: Which month did Kamal join the agency?
qa.a: Kamal joined in June.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling about losing the agency line on his CV?
qa.a: Kamal may be afraid of losing it while also feeling used, though Rukmini admits she can't tell if he is afraid, angry or resolved.

qa.q: What should Kamal do if nothing changes by the date in his notebook?
qa.a: Kamal should walk away as planned and keep the updated CV and other applications moving, since he has asked his questions and set a limit.

qa.q: How does Rukmini seem to see Kamal's situation?
qa.a: Rukmini seems sympathetic and watchful; she notices the long hours, the missing stipend and the vague answers, but is careful not to claim she knows what Kamal feels.

grounding: An unpaid full-time intern feels used but fears losing the CV line, asks about stipend and learning goals and sets a time limit.

passage: Faculty coordinator's note, Vandana. Payal came to office hours on Wednesday, twisting the strap of her bag. She said the firm where she interns reminds her every week that they are "doing her a favour" by taking her on. She stays until midnight, and last week ran the owner's personal errands, and she feels she cannot say no. When I asked what she was getting in return, in learning or a stipend, she went quiet and said, "They have done so much for me." She looked grateful and confused at once. I explained that a fair deal means effort in return for learning or pay, and that being done a favour cannot wipe out her rights. I did not decide for her. We wrote down her tasks and three learning goals to raise with her supervisor. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: Which day did Payal come to office hours?
qa.a: Payal came on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she said "They have done so much for me"?
qa.a: Payal looked grateful and confused at once, and felt she could not say no.

qa.q: What would you advise Payal to raise with her supervisor?
qa.a: Payal could raise her list of tasks and the three learning goals she wrote with Vandana, since an honest exchange is work for learning or pay.

qa.q: How might the firm see its own favour to Payal?
qa.a: The firm seems to see it as a favour that Payal should repay with endless effort, while Vandana's view is that a favour does not cancel her rights.

grounding: A firm says it does Payal a favour by taking her on; Payal feels indebted, and a coordinator helps her separate gratitude from servitude.

passage: In her second week at the marketing firm, Sudha sat beside Tanvir Kaur for forty minutes over a spreadsheet. "Try it first, then I'll show you," Tanvir Ma'am said. It was the first real task Sudha had been given: the client's monthly report. When the numbers came out wrong, Tanvir Ma'am did not sigh. She circled one cell and asked, "What do you think happened here?" Sudha found the slip herself. On her last Friday, Sudha asked shyly for a reference and for feedback, and Tanvir Ma'am listed two things to work on. That evening Sudha texted a friend that she wanted to be exactly like her manager, then paused and wrote her own plan: message every month, prepare for the other interview, finish her own project.

qa.q: How long did Tanvir Ma'am sit with Sudha over the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Tanvir Ma'am sat with Sudha for forty minutes.

qa.q: Why does Sudha want to be exactly like her manager?
qa.a: Sudha admires Tanvir Ma'am's patience, since she taught properly, gave a real task and did not sigh at the wrong numbers.

qa.q: What could Sudha do with the two things Tanvir Ma'am listed?
qa.a: Sudha could work on them and share the progress in her monthly messages, so the feedback is taken seriously and the relationship continues.

qa.q: How might Tanvir Ma'am see Sudha?
qa.a: Tanvir Ma'am may see a keen learner who tries things first and takes correction well, which fits her patient way of teaching.

grounding: A manager teaches Sudha properly with real tasks; Sudha admires her, asks for a reference and feedback and plans to keep in touch while looking after her own needs.
